  "text": "During the winter, Mara’s mother had begun sending photographs of the garden. Most showed little more than wet paving and the bare stems along the fence. In one, a blackbird stood beside an overturned flowerpot, looking as if it had been caught doing something it would not explain. Mara saved that one to her phone.

Her mother had always known what to do in the garden. She grew beans against the fence and put in bulbs each autumn, even in years when she complained there was no point. When Mara was small, she had been given the job of carrying a bucket for weeds. She could still remember its metal handle pressing a line into her palm.

Now her mother mentioned the garden less often. On their calls, she talked about the price of milk or the new timetable at the library. If Mara asked whether she had been outside, her mother said it was too cold, or that the ground was too soft. Once she said she had gone as far as the shed and come back because she had forgotten why she was there.

Mara considered offering to visit, but her mother had not asked. She had always disliked having help arranged for her. At Christmas, she had insisted on making lunch herself, then let Mara dry the dishes without comment. They had stood together at the sink, looking out at the garden after the light had gone. Mara could see her own face in the window and, beyond it, the pale square of the shed."
